summary: Specifies the Online Certificate Status Protocol, which lets a client ask a server about the current status of a digital certificate without downloading certificate revocation lists. It was replaced by RFC 6960 and updated by RFC 6277.

plainLanguage.summary: OCSP is a way of asking about one certificate at a time. Instead of downloading a list of every certificate that has been withdrawn, a client sends the certificate's serial number to a server and gets back a signed answer saying whether it is still valid.

questions: how to check if a certificate is revoked
subtitle: Asking a server whether a certificate has been withdrawn, instead of downloading a list.

tldr.problem: A certificate that has been withdrawn must not keep being trusted, but a certificate authority publishes revocations as a list that grows and is signed periodically. Checking that list for one certificate means downloading it, and the information it holds can be days old.
tldr.mechanism: OCSP lets a client ask a responder about one certificate at a time. The request identifies the certificate by its serial number and hashes of the issuer's name and key, and the responder returns a signed answer saying the certificate is good, revoked or unknown, with the times the answer applies.
tldr.outcome: The response can be signed by the authority itself or by a responder the authority has authorised with a special certificate. The RFC also lists the extensions a client and responder can use, including a nonce that ties a response to its request.

today: RFC 2560 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 6960 and updated by RFC 6277.

sections.title: Why a Status Protocol
sections.content:
In lieu of, or as a supplement to, checking against a periodic certificate revocation list, it may be necessary to obtain timely information about the revocation status of a certificate. The RFC gives high-value funds transfer and large stock trades as examples.

The Online Certificate Status Protocol enables applications to determine the revocation state of an identified certificate. It may be used to satisfy some of the operational requirements of providing more timely revocation information than is possible with revocation lists, and it may also be used to obtain additional status information. An OCSP client issues a status request to an OCSP responder and suspends acceptance of the certificate in question until the responder provides a response.

The protocol specifies the data that has to be exchanged between an application checking the status of a certificate and the server providing that status. A request carries the protocol version, the service request, the target certificate identifier and optional extensions the responder may process. On receipt, the responder checks whether the message is well formed, whether it is configured to provide the requested service, and whether the request holds the information the responder needs. If any of those fail, the responder produces an error message; otherwise it returns a definitive response.

A definitive response is always digitally signed. The signing key must belong to the authority that issued the certificate, to a trusted responder whose public key the requester already trusts, or to a designated responder that holds a specially marked certificate issued directly by the authority.
sections.plainLanguage: Revocation lists are published on a schedule, so they can be out of date, and they cover every certificate a given authority has issued. OCSP asks a question about one certificate and gets an answer about that certificate alone.

sections.title: Checking a Response Before Trusting It
sections.content:
Before accepting a signed response as valid, an OCSP client must confirm six things. The certificate identified in the response must correspond to the one identified in the request. The signature on the response must be valid. The identity of the signer must match the intended recipient of the request. The signer must currently be authorised to sign the response. The time at which the status is known to be correct must be sufficiently recent. And, when it is available, the time at or before which newer information will be available must be greater than the current time.

The key that signs a certificate's status information need not be the key that signed the certificate, but the entity signing it must be authorised to do so. The issuer must either sign the responses itself or explicitly delegate that authority. The delegation is marked by including id-kp-OCSPSigning in an extendedKeyUsage extension in the responder's certificate, and that certificate must be issued directly by the authority that issued the certificate in question.

Systems that rely on OCSP must be able to detect and enforce that delegation, and must reject a response if the certificate needed to validate the signature fails at least one of three tests. It must match a local configuration of OCSP signing authority for the certificate in question, or it must be the certificate of the authority that issued the certificate in question, or it must include the id-ad-ocspSigning value in an extendedKeyUsage extension and be issued by that authority.

Because an authorised responder gives status information for one or more authorities, clients need a way to check that the responder's own certificate has not been revoked. The RFC gives a CA three choices. It can say the client may trust the responder for the life of the responder's certificate, by including the id-pkix-ocsp-nocheck extension, which should be non-critical with a NULL value; a compromise of such a key is as serious as a compromise of the key used to sign revocation lists. It can specify how the responder's certificate should be checked, using CRL Distribution Points or Authority Information Access. Or it can specify nothing, leaving the decision to the client's own security policy.
sections.plainLanguage: A signed answer is only worth something if you check who signed it and whether the answer is fresh. A responder can be authorised by the authority, and the client must check that authorisation, using its own certificate rules.

sections.title: The Request
sections.content:
The syntax is written in ASN.1, and the data to be signed is encoded using the distinguished encoding rules. ASN.1 explicit tagging is used as a default unless specified otherwise. The actual formatting of the message may vary with the transport used, and the RFC names HTTP, SMTP and LDAP as possibilities.

An OCSPRequest holds a TBSRequest and an optional signature. The TBSRequest holds a version, defaulting to v1, an optional requestor name, a list of requests and optional extensions. Each request holds a certificate identifier and optional per-request extensions.

The certificate identifier, or CertID, is how the certificate is named. It holds a hash algorithm identifier, the hash of the issuer's distinguished name, the hash of the issuer's public key, and the serial number of the certificate being asked about. The issuer's name hash is calculated over the DER encoding of the issuer's name field in the certificate being checked. The issuer's key hash is calculated over the value, excluding the tag and length, of the subject public key field in the issuer's certificate. The same hash algorithm is used for both hashes and is named in the hash algorithm field.

The RFC explains why both hashes are used. It is possible for two certificate authorities to choose the same name, because uniqueness in the name is a recommendation that cannot be enforced. Two authorities will never, however, have the same public key unless they deliberately shared the private key or one of the keys was compromised.

Support for any specific extension is optional and the critical flag should not be set. Unrecognised extensions must be ignored unless they have the critical flag set and are not understood. The requestor may choose to sign the request, in which case the signature is computed over the TBSRequest, the requestor must give its name in the requestorName field, and it may include certificates that help the responder check the signature.
sections.plainLanguage: The request names the certificate by three things: a number that only its issuer uses, plus two hashes of the issuer, one of its name and one of its key. Together those make sure the answer is about the certificate you meant.

sections.title: The Response
sections.content:
An OCSP response at a minimum carries a response status giving the processing status of the prior request. If that status is one of the error conditions, the response bytes are not set. The response bytes hold an object identifier and the response itself, encoded as an octet string. For a basic responder the type is id-pkix-ocsp-basic, and both responders and clients must handle that type.

The basic response holds the response data, a signature algorithm identifier, the signature, computed over the hash of the DER encoding of the response data, and optionally certificates. The response data holds a version, the identity of the responder, the time the response was produced, a list of single responses and optional extensions. The responder is identified either by name or by a key hash, which is the SHA-1 hash of the responder's public key excluding the tag and length fields.

Each single response holds the certificate identifier, the status, the time the status is known to be correct, an optional time by which newer information will be available, and optional extensions. The status itself is one of three values.

The good state indicates a positive answer to the status inquiry. At a minimum it says the certificate is not revoked, but it does not necessarily mean the certificate was ever issued or that the time the response was produced falls within the certificate's validity interval. Response extensions may convey additional assertions about issuance and validity. The revoked state says the certificate has been revoked, either permanently or temporarily on hold. The unknown state says the responder does not know about the certificate being asked about.

Three times appear in a response. ThisUpdate is the time at which the status being indicated is known to be correct. NextUpdate is the time at or before which newer information will be available about the status of the certificate. ProducedAt is the time at which the responder signed the response. If nextUpdate is not set, the responder is indicating that newer revocation information is available all the time.

Responders may pre-produce signed responses for a stated time, and the same three fields record when the status was known to be correct, when newer information will be available, and when the response was produced.
sections.plainLanguage: The answer comes back signed, and says one of three things: the certificate is fine, the certificate has been withdrawn, or the server has never heard of it. It also says how fresh the answer is and when to expect a newer one.

sections.title: Extensions
sections.content:
The extensions are based on the extension model used in X.509 version 3 certificates, and support for all of them is optional for both clients and responders.

The nonce cryptographically binds a request and a response together, to prevent replay attacks. It is included as one of the request extensions in a request and as one of the response extensions in a response, identified in both by the object identifier id-pkix-ocsp-nonce.

CRL references let the responder indicate which revocation list a revoked or held certificate is found on, which is useful when OCSP is used between repositories and as an auditing mechanism. The list may be named by a URL, by a number or by a time, and the extension is identified by id-pkix-ocsp-crl.

Acceptable response types let a client say which kinds of response it understands, using the extension id-pkix-ocsp-response whose value is a sequence of object identifiers.

The archive cutoff lets a responder keep revocation information beyond a certificate's expiry. The date obtained by subtracting the retention interval from the producedAt time in a response is the certificate's archive cutoff date. Applications use it to show that a digital signature was, or was not, reliable on the day it was produced, even if the certificate has long since expired. The extension is identified by id-pkix-ocsp-archive-cutoff and has the syntax of a generalized time. The RFC's example is a server run with a seven-year retention policy, where the value would be the producedAt time minus seven years.

All the extensions specified as CRL entry extensions are also supported as single extensions. The service locator is for a server that receives a request and routes it to the server that is authoritative for the certificate, and it is included among the per-request extensions.
sections.plainLanguage: Extensions add optional extras. The most useful is the nonce, a random value that the server echoes back so that an old answer cannot be replayed later. Another tells the client where to find the revocation list the answer came from.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
For the service to be effective, certificate-using systems must connect to the certificate status service provider. If that connection cannot be obtained, certificate-using systems could implement revocation list processing logic as a fallback.

The RFC points out a denial of service vulnerability in the face of a flood of queries. Producing a cryptographic signature significantly affects the response generation cycle time, which makes the situation worse. Unsigned error responses open the protocol to another denial of service attack, in which an attacker sends false error responses.

The use of precomputed responses allows replay attacks, in which an old good response is replayed before its expiration date but after the certificate has been revoked. Deployments of OCSP should carefully evaluate the benefit of precomputed responses against the probability of a replay attack and the costs of a successful one.

Requests do not contain the responder they are directed to, which allows an attacker to replay a request to any number of responders. The reliance on HTTP caching in some deployment scenarios may also result in unexpected results if intermediate servers are incorrectly configured or known to have cache management faults, so implementors are advised to take the reliability of HTTP cache mechanisms into account when deploying OCSP over HTTP.
sections.plainLanguage: Signing every answer is expensive, so a flood of questions can tie up the server. Answering from a pre-signed store is cheaper but lets an old answer be replayed after a certificate has been withdrawn.

messages.label: OCSP Request
messages.note: Carries the serial number and the hashes of the issuer's name and key.

messages.label: OCSP Response
messages.note: A signed status of good, revoked or unknown, with the times it applies.

items.title: good
items.text: The certificate is not revoked. This does not necessarily mean it was ever issued or that it is within its validity period.

items.title: revoked
items.text: The certificate has been revoked, either permanently or temporarily on hold.

items.title: unknown
items.text: The responder does not know about the certificate being asked about.

items.label: Valid confirmations
items.desc: The response carries the statuses that were asked for.

items.label: Illegal confirmation request
items.desc: The request does not conform to the OCSP syntax.

items.label: Internal error in issuer
items.desc: The responder reached an inconsistent internal state. The query should be retried.

items.label: Try again later
items.desc: The service exists but is temporarily unable to respond.

items.label: Must sign the request
items.desc: The server requires the client to sign the request.

items.label: Request unauthorized
items.desc: The client is not authorized to make this query to this server.
